title: Rejoice, Pray, and Learn Contentment
summary: Paul urges the church to stand firm, pleads with two women leaders to agree in the Lord, and calls everyone to rejoice, to be gentle, to pray instead of worrying, and to fill their minds with what is true and good. He then thanks the Philippians for their gift, explaining that he has learned the secret of contentment in plenty and in need through Christ who strengthens him. The letter ends with greetings, including from believers in Caesar's household.
story: The letter's last chapter gathers its threads. The call to stand firm in the Lord follows directly from the end of chapter 3, where believers are citizens of heaven awaiting their Savior. The plea to Euodia and Syntyche applies the call to unity and the mind of Christ from chapter 2 to two real people. The command to rejoice repeats the letter's leading note. And the thank-you for the gift, which Paul saved for last, completes the partnership in the gospel he mentioned in the opening lines (1:5). Epaphroditus, whose illness and return were described in chapter 2, is named as the one who brought the gift.
historical:
The chapter looks back on more than a decade of friendship. Paul founded the church around AD 49 or 50 (Acts 16). When he left Macedonia, the Philippians alone supported him financially, and even while he was in Thessalonica, soon after leaving Philippi, they sent help more than once (verses 15 and 16; compare 2 Corinthians 11:9). There had then been a period when they had no opportunity to help (verse 10), and now they had sent a gift by Epaphroditus to Paul in prison.

The household of Caesar (verse 22) did not mean the emperor's family but the large staff of slaves and freedmen who served the imperial administration, many of them in responsible posts. They worked in Rome and in the provinces. Their greeting fits a Roman imprisonment naturally, but members of the imperial household were also found in cities like Ephesus, so it does not settle the question of where Paul was held. The Clement of verse 3 is otherwise unknown; later tradition sometimes identified him with Clement, a leader of the church in Rome at the end of the first century, but there is little evidence for this.
cultural:
Women held a notable place in the church at Philippi from its beginning, when Lydia and other women gathered at a place of prayer by the river were the first converts (Acts 16:13-15). Euodia and Syntyche had labored side by side with Paul in the gospel, the same language of fellow athletes contending together that he uses in 1:27. Their disagreement mattered because they were leaders. Paul does not take sides; he pleads with each by name. The true yokefellow he asks to help them is not named. Suggestions include Epaphroditus, Luke, Timothy, or the church as a whole, and some have wondered whether Syzygus was a personal name, which Paul would be playing on by calling him true to his name.

Paul's language about contentment borrows from the philosophy of the day. Autarkes, self-sufficient or content, was a favorite word of the Stoics, who taught that a wise person should need nothing outside himself. Paul uses the word but changes its source: his sufficiency comes from Christ, who strengthens him. The verb for having learned the secret (verse 12) was used of initiation into the mystery religions. Friendship and gift-giving in the Greco-Roman world also carried expectations of return and obligation, which may explain why Paul thanks the Philippians so carefully, avoiding any suggestion that he is angling for more and describing their gift as an offering to God.
literary: The chapter has two main parts: final appeals (verses 1 to 9) and a thank-you note (verses 10 to 20), followed by greetings (verses 21 to 23). The appeals move from a specific conflict to general commands, each short and memorable: rejoice, be gentle, do not be anxious, pray, think on these things, put it into practice. Verse 8 is a list of six virtues, each introduced by whatever, followed by a summary of two more, which reads like the lists of virtues in the moral philosophy of the time. The thank-you section is carefully balanced: Paul rejoices in the gift (verse 10), insists he did not need it (verses 11 to 13), affirms that they did well to send it (verse 14), recalls their history of giving (verses 15 and 16), and then reframes the gift as fruit to their account and a sacrifice to God (verses 17 and 18). It closes with a promise (verse 19) and a doxology (verse 20), a short burst of praise to God.

outline.t: Stand firm, and a plea to Euodia and Syntyche
Rejoice, and pray instead of worrying
Think on what is true and good, and put it into practice
Thanks for the Philippians' partnership and gift

doctrines.note: Paul's remedy for anxiety is prayer with thanksgiving, bringing every request to God (verse 6). The promise is not that every request will be granted as asked, but that the peace of God will guard the heart and mind in Christ Jesus (verse 7).

God will supply all your needs according to his glorious riches in Christ Jesus (verse 19). Paul speaks from experience of both hunger and plenty; God's provision does not mean the absence of hardship but his sufficiency in every circumstance.

The church at Philippi is a partnership in giving and receiving. Its unity matters enough for Paul to name two leaders who disagree and to ask others to help them reconcile. Material support for gospel work is described as worship, a fragrant offering to God (verse 18).

words.note: Merimnao, to worry or be anxious. The word can describe proper concern: Paul uses it positively of Timothy's care for the Philippians (2:20). Here it means the anxious care that divides the mind. Jesus used the same verb in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:25-34). Paul's command is not a demand to feel nothing but a direction: turn the worry into prayer.

Autarkes, content or self-sufficient. In Stoic philosophy the word described the wise person who is independent of circumstances. Paul claims the same freedom from circumstances, but not by self-reliance: the next verse says the strength comes from Christ. Contentment for Paul is learned, not natural.

Endunamoo, to strengthen or empower. The present participle in verse 13 describes Christ as the one who keeps on giving strength. In context the all things Paul can do are the things he has just listed: going hungry, having plenty, living humbly, and living in abundance. The verse is about endurance and contentment, not a promise of success in any goal.

christ: In this chapter Christ is the one in whom believers stand firm, rejoice, and find peace. The peace of God guards hearts and minds in Christ Jesus (verse 7). The Lord is near (verse 5), which can mean near in presence or near in his coming, and both carry weight. Above all, Christ is the source of Paul's contentment: “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (verse 13). The strength is not a tool for ambition but the power to be content in any condition, the same pattern of self-giving and trust seen in Christ himself in chapter 2. God's provision comes according to his glorious riches in Christ Jesus (verse 19), and the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is the letter's last word.
questions: Paul names two people in conflict and asks others to help them. Why is it so hard to help friends reconcile, and what might that help look like?
What would it mean in practice to turn a specific worry into prayer with thanksgiving this week?
Paul says he learned contentment in both hunger and plenty. Which is harder for you to be content in, and why?
